site.title: P9 — Mars Rover Autonomy
site.subtitle: Autonomous manipulation and workflow automation for the FHNW Mars Rover
site.description: Companion site to the FHNW master’s thesis P9 — Mars Rover Autonomy: a SmolVLA policy post-trained with RECAP, n8n workflow automation over ROS 2, and TensorRT deployment on the Jetson Orin. With two demos you can drive yourself.

hero.eyebrow: FHNW · School of Engineering · Master’s thesis
hero.lead: A vision-language-action policy, and the workflow layer that commands it — on a rover that competes at the European Rover Challenge.
hero.imageAlt: The FHNW Mars Rover with its six-degree-of-freedom manipulator

overview.heading: One manipulator, two ways to command it
body: The FHNW Rover Team competes in the European Rover Challenge, where one of the tasks is operating a maintenance panel. Building on a ROS 2 stack that already ran per-task imitation policies, this thesis rebuilds how that manipulator is commanded — a policy that takes an instruction, and a workflow layer that composes the sequences around it.
The report covers all of this in detail. This page is for the parts a PDF cannot hold: a rover you can send somewhere, workflows you can open, and a policy you can argue with.

pillars.title: SmolVLA, post-trained with RECAP
pillars.body: A single SmolVLA policy conditioned on a natural-language task description replaces the per-task ACT models of the previous project, post-trained with RECAP, an advantage-conditioned reinforcement-learning recipe. It is re-tasked by changing the instruction rather than by loading another model.

metric.label: average LIBERO success, from 62.9 %
metric.note: One full pass around the RECAP loop, rollout collection included.

pillars.question: RQ1 · task automation and reinforcement learning

pillars.title: n8n workflows over ROS 2
pillars.body: n8n is bridged to ROS 2 over rosbridge, giving operators a no-code way to compose task sequences from topics, services and actions, with the required order of operations enforced. An LLM agent built inside n8n answers free-text questions by calling those same tools, and a small fine-tuned model runs it on board at no per-call cost.

metric.label: tool calls on 43 held-out prompts
metric.note: Against the cloud configuration’s 92 %: fine-tuning closed the gap, it did not overtake it.

pillars.question: RQ1 · task automation, RQ3 · order enforcement and human-in-the-loop

smaller.title: Real-time deployment
smaller.label: per chunk, ≈3 Hz replanning
smaller.body: Compiled to TensorRT as a VLM prefix and an action expert at different precisions, which is what fits the policy into the control cycle on the Jetson Orin.

smaller.title: Depth sensing
smaller.label: added to the state vector
smaller.body: The gripper’s 8×8 time-of-flight grid enters the policy through one configuration entry. Whether the policy is better for it was not measured; the ablation is future work.

smaller.title: Visual servoing
smaller.label: median error, 25 mm required
smaller.body: A classical approach phase for targets language cannot name precisely — “the third switch from the left” — handing the policy a consistent starting pose.

demos.title: A virtual rover, driven by n8n
demos.body: A simulated rover offering real ROS 2 topics, services and actions, driven by eleven n8n workflows — and a read-only live view anyone can open. Send it to the lake from your phone, watch the battery watchdog preempt a patrol, or ask the agent what interfaces the robot has.
points: Live view of the robot, read-only at the protocol level
All eleven workflows on a real n8n canvas
The n8n editor, the drive form, and the agent chat

demos.title: SmolVLA + RECAP + guidance, client-side
demos.body: The policy family from the first of the two systems, solving PushT entirely in the browser: Chipmunk2D physics as WASM, inference on WebGPU. Drag the agent away and watch the policy recover; move the guidance weight and watch what it does — and does not — change.
points: Take over from the policy mid-episode
Sampled action chunks drawn on the arena
Guidance weight and the denoising steps, both scrubable

demos.title: Browse the demonstrations the policy learned from
demos.body: Every episode the manipulator was taught, in LeRobot’s dataset viewer: camera streams, joint states and actions, scrubbable frame by frame. This is the raw material behind the policy — what a demonstration actually looks like, including the ones where the operator fumbled.
points: Camera and state streams, synchronised per frame
Episode by episode, no download required

supporting.heading: Manipulator control and safety gating
body: The six-degree-of-freedom manipulator is driven with FZI’s Cartesian controllers, extended here with a per-joint weighting that damps the forearm roll so it no longer absorbs wrist rotations, and mirrored by a MuJoCo model for smoke tests.

Both autonomous control modes are gated. A heartbeat from the operator station must be present, so a lost link halts autonomous motion without anyone having to act, and a latching software e-stop aborts the running policy or alignment goal and refuses new ones until it is reset.
supporting.note: Described last in the report as the supporting work it is, rather than as a contribution of its own.

results.eyebrow: End to end, on the arm
results.heading: What it actually does
results.body: The pipeline is demonstrated end to end on the manipulator. The deployed policy turns a rotary panel switch on roughly four attempts in five — below a teleoperating human, but repeatable until it succeeds. Lever switches, whose motion first tensions and then snaps over, are harder and carry fewer demonstrations.
results.open: Plug insertion is the one substep still open, and for a reason worth stating plainly: an operator cannot teleoperate it well enough to demonstrate it, so there is nothing to imitate. A purpose-built tool now exists but has not yet been used to record it.

libero.heading: What the policy learned, and what it did not
libero.note: Evaluation episodes of the policies compared in the report. Filenames in the source encode policy, task, outcome and episode; these are three pairs where the difference is visible rather than statistical.

pairs.title: A skill only co-training recovers
pairs.task: GOAL suite — “open the middle drawer of the cabinet”
pairs.body: The skill is present in the expert demonstrations and absent from the base policy’s own rollouts. Rollout data sharpens behaviour a policy already shows; behaviour it lacks has to come back from the demonstrations, which is what co-training mixes in.

clips.label: Base policy
clips.caption: The gripper hovers in front of the cabinet, never engages the handle, and the episode runs out.

clips.label: Co-trained
clips.caption: The gripper reaches the handle and pulls the drawer open.

pairs.title: Where long horizons break down
pairs.task: LONG suite — one subgoal against two
pairs.body: The suite average is dragged down by instructions that chain two subgoals, because the error of each compounds. Single-subgoal tasks in the same suite reach 70–80 %.

clips.label: One subgoal
clips.caption: “Pick up the book and place it in the back compartment of the caddy.” The policy completes it.

clips.label: Two subgoals
clips.caption: “Put both the alphabet soup and the cream cheese box in the basket.” The first object is placed, the second is never picked up.

pairs.title: The two RECAP variants do not agree everywhere
pairs.task: SPATIAL suite — the same task, two post-training recipes
pairs.body: Co-training is not uniformly better. On this SPATIAL task the rollout-only policy succeeds where the co-trained one fails — a reminder that the suite averages in the report are averages, and that SPATIAL is the suite most sensitive to guidance.

clips.label: Co-trained
clips.caption: The same task the rollout-only policy completes.

clips.label: Rollout-only
clips.caption: Reaches, grasps and transports the bowl.
